title: The Lie bracket of an associative algebra is the commutator
content: On any associative algebra Mathlib equips the additive group with a Lie-ring structure whose bracket is the commutator: ⁅X, Y⁆ = X·Y − Y·X (LieRing.of_associative_ring_bracket). Rewriting with this lemma and sub_eq_zero turns 'bracket vanishes' into 'X·Y = Y·X', which is definitionally Commute X Y. So lie_eq_zero_iff_commute records the algebraic hinge of the whole file: the Lie-algebra structure (bracket) and the multiplicative structure (commutativity) agree exactly on the vanishing locus. This is the link that makes the exponential multiplicative in the next section.
mathContext: $\lbrack X, Y\rbrack = X Y - Y X$, hence $\lbrack X, Y\rbrack = 0 \iff XY = YX \iff \operatorname{Commute} X\, Y$.

title: Vanishing bracket ⇒ the exponential is multiplicative
content: exp_add_of_lie_eq_zero feeds commute_of_lie_eq_zero into Mathlib's NormedSpace.exp_add_of_commute to conclude exp(X+Y) = exp X · exp Y whenever ⁅X,Y⁆ = 0. Over a real Banach algebra (ℝ is RCLike, 𝔸 a complete normed algebra) this is the verified, finite-radius form of the Lie-theoretic fact that an abelian Lie subalgebra integrates to an abelian subgroup. It is exactly the exponential-map identity the parent entry's narrative invokes but does not prove.
mathContext: $\lbrack X, Y\rbrack = 0 \implies \exp(X+Y) = \exp(X)\exp(Y)$ in a real Banach algebra.

title: The one-parameter subgroup t ↦ exp(t·X) and its homomorphism laws
content: oneParam X t := exp ℝ (t • X) is the one-parameter subgroup generated by the infinitesimal generator X — the image under the exponential map of the line ℝ·X in the Lie algebra. Its homomorphism laws are the 'exponential map properties' the open question asks to state: oneParam_zero (γ(0) = 1, from exp_zero), oneParam_add (γ(s+t) = γ(s)·γ(t), since s•X and t•X commute as scalar multiples of X), oneParam_neg_mul (γ(−t)·γ(t) = 1, so every element is invertible), and oneParam_commute (the image is abelian). Together they exhibit γ_X as a homomorphism (ℝ,+) → (𝔸,×) — the concrete object Hilbert's 5th problem is ultimately about.
